topics.name: Potassium
topics.kicker: Element 19 · The soft alkali metal in bananas, nerves, and fertilizer
topics.briefing: Potassium is a metal so soft you can cut it with a knife, and so reactive that it bursts into lilac-colored flames when dropped into water. Humphry Davy first isolated it in 1807 by running electricity through melted caustic potash, a chemical made from the wood ashes that gave the element its name. Your nerves and heart depend on potassium ions, and bananas are a famous source.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Humphry Davy reportedly danced around his laboratory with joy when tiny globules of this metal burst into flame as he passed current from a huge battery through its molten hydroxide. In October 1807, it became the first metal ever isolated by electrolysis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 19, whose name comes from potash.

tossups.p: Jens Christian Skou shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering an enzyme that uses energy from ATP to pump three sodium ions out of a cell while bringing two ions of this element in.
tossups.r: This element gives a lilac color in a flame test. For 10 points, name this element, whose ions are concentrated inside cells and are found in foods like bananas.

tossups.p: Roderick MacKinnon shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for revealing the structure of channels that let ions of this element, but not smaller sodium ions, pass through cell membranes. Ions of this element flow out of a neuron to reset it after an action potential.
tossups.r: Bananas are a famous food source of this element. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 19.

tossups.p: Most of the argon in Earth’s atmosphere was made by the radioactive decay of this element’s isotope with mass number 40. Geologists use that same decay, which has a half-life of about 1.25 billion years, to find the ages of volcanic rocks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 19, an alkali metal found in bananas.

tossups.p: A radioactive isotope of this element is the largest natural source of radioactivity inside the human body. Because bananas are rich in this element, scientists jokingly measure tiny radiation doses in a unit called the “banana equivalent dose.”
tossups.r: Humphry Davy isolated this element in 1807 from potash. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 19.

tossups.p: A chlorate of this element supplies oxygen in match heads, and heating that chlorate with a catalyst is a classic way to make oxygen in the lab. Gunpowder, first made in China, is about three-quarters saltpeter, a nitrate of this element, mixed with charcoal and sulfur.
tossups.r: This element’s flame test gives a lilac color. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 19.

tossups.p: The superoxide of this element is used in breathing equipment and spacecraft because it reacts with exhaled water and carbon dioxide to release oxygen. A liquid alloy of sodium and this element has been used to cool some nuclear reactors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this soft alkali metal that sits just below sodium on the periodic table.

tossups.p: Cream of tartar, used by bakers to stabilize whipped egg whites, is a salt of tartaric acid and this element. Crystals of that salt form naturally inside barrels as grape juice ferments into wine.
tossups.r: This element’s ions are found in bananas, potatoes, and spinach. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 19.

tossups.p: After nuclear accidents, people living nearby may take pills of an iodide of this element to keep radioactive iodine out of their thyroid glands. A chloride of this element is sold as a salt substitute for people who need to eat less sodium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 19, which reacts with water to give a lilac flame.

tossups.p: Canada’s province of Saskatchewan has huge underground deposits of sylvite, a chloride mineral of this element left behind when an ancient sea dried up. Sylvite is mined to make fertilizer, because plants need this element along with nitrogen and phosphorus.
tossups.r: Its name comes from “pot ash.” For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 19.

tossups.p: Atoms of this element are the first to place an electron in a 4s orbital, before any 3d orbitals fill. This element’s single valence electron is held so loosely that it reacts with water even faster than sodium does.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 19, whose symbol comes from the Latin word kalium.

tossups.p: Doctors call a high level of this element in the blood hyperkalemia, a word built from this element’s Latin name. Both too much and too little of this element can disturb the rhythm of the heart, whose muscle cells depend on its ions.
tossups.r: Bananas are a famous food source of this nutrient. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 19.

tossups.p: A deep purple compound of this element and manganese is a strong oxidizing agent used to treat water. In some titrations, that compound is its own indicator, since a faint pink color lingers once it is in excess.
tossups.r: Fertilizers supply this element to plants, along with nitrogen and phosphorus. For 10 points, name this alkali metal, element 19, which sits between sodium and rubidium in group 1.

tossups.p: Old samples of this soft metal can grow a dangerous crust of superoxide, so chemists store it under mineral oil to keep out oxygen and moisture. When dropped into water, it skates across the surface as the hydrogen it releases catches fire.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this alkali metal, which gives a lilac color in a flame test.

tossups.p: The first patent issued in the United States, in 1790, was for a better way to make a carbonate of this element. Early American settlers made that product for soap and glass by soaking wood ashes in water, then boiling the liquid down in pots.
tossups.r: That product, potash, gives this element its name. For 10 points, name this alkali metal with atomic number 19.

clues.t: Element with atomic number 19; its symbol comes from the Latin word kalium
An alkali metal in group 1, just below sodium and above rubidium
Bananas, potatoes, and spinach are good food sources of its ions
Gives a lilac (pale violet) color in a flame test
Named for potash, the “pot ash” made by boiling down water that had soaked through wood ashes
Humphry Davy isolated it in 1807 by electrolysis of molten caustic potash, the first metal isolated that way
Reacts with water so fast that the hydrogen released catches fire, so it is stored under mineral oil
A metal so soft it can be cut with a knife
Its ions flow out of neurons to reset them after an action potential and help keep the heartbeat steady
A protein pump uses ATP to move 3 sodium ions out of a cell and 2 of its ions in
One of the three main plant nutrients in fertilizer, with nitrogen and phosphorus
Saltpeter, its nitrate, makes up about three-quarters of gunpowder
Its radioactive isotope with mass number 40 decays into argon, letting geologists date volcanic rocks
The first element to put an electron in a 4s orbital
Most argon in Earth’s air came from decay of its radioactive isotope, which has a half-life of about 1.25 billion years
Bananas’ radioactivity inspired the playful “banana equivalent dose”; its isotope is the body’s biggest natural radiation source
Jens Christian Skou shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering the pump that brings its ions into cells
Roderick MacKinnon shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing how channels let its ions pass but not sodium’s
Its superoxide reacts with exhaled breath to release oxygen in spacecraft and breathing gear
A liquid alloy with sodium, called NaK, has cooled some nuclear reactors
Cream of tartar, used to stabilize whipped egg whites, is its salt of tartaric acid
Pills of its iodide protect the thyroid after nuclear accidents; its chloride is a salt substitute
Sylvite, its chloride mineral, is mined in huge amounts in Saskatchewan, Canada
Too much of it in the blood is called hyperkalemia, a word built from its Latin name
Its deep purple permanganate is a strong oxidizing agent used in titrations and water treatment
The first U.S. patent (1790) was for a better way to make potash
Its chlorate supplies oxygen in match heads and releases oxygen when heated with a catalyst

trap.title: Not sodium!
trap.body: Sodium sits right above this element in group 1, and the two share many clues: both are soft enough to cut, both react violently with water, both were first isolated by Humphry Davy in 1807, and the same pump moves both across cell membranes. Their symbols are another trap, because neither one matches its English name.
trap.fix: A lilac flame, element 19, potash, bananas, saltpeter, and argon-40 dating point here, and this element’s symbol comes from kalium. A bright yellow-orange flame, element 11, table salt, and caustic soda point to sodium, whose symbol, Na, comes from natrium.

topics.name: Ammonia
topics.kicker: Nitrogen plus three hydrogens · The pungent gas behind most fertilizer
topics.briefing: Ammonia is a sharp-smelling gas made of one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms, and you may know its sting from glass cleaners. Around 1909, Fritz Haber figured out how to make it from the nitrogen in air, and Carl Bosch scaled the process up in giant factories. Fertilizer made from that ammonia helps grow food for billions of people, which makes it one of the most important chemicals on Earth.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Charles Townes built the first maser in the 1950s using molecules of this compound, which flip inside out like an umbrella in the wind about 24 billion times a second. That flip happens as the molecule’s nitrogen atom tunnels from one side of the molecule to the other.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pungent compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, made by the Haber process.

tossups.p: Ernest Solvay’s process for making sodium carbonate, or soda ash, uses and recycles this compound. In the Ostwald [“OST-vahlt”] process, this compound is burned over a platinum catalyst as the first step in making nitric acid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound made from nitrogen and hydrogen in the Haber process.

tossups.p: Carl Bosch shared the 1931 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for high-pressure methods that let factories make this compound on a huge scale. Fritz Haber won the 1918 prize for making this compound directly from its elements.
tossups.r: Most of this compound becomes fertilizer. For 10 points, name this pungent gas, whose molecules contain three hydrogen atoms.

tossups.p: In a classic demonstration of Graham’s law, cotton balls soaked in this compound and in hydrochloric acid are placed at opposite ends of a glass tube. A white ring forms closer to the hydrochloric acid end, because this lighter gas diffuses faster.
tossups.r: That white ring is a chloride salt. For 10 points, name this pungent weak base, which is made by the Haber process.

tossups.p: In the “fountain” experiment, water sprays up into a flask of this gas, which dissolves in water so readily that it leaves a partial vacuum behind. A few drops of phenolphthalein turn the fountain pink, because this gas makes water basic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pungent compound of one nitrogen and three hydrogen atoms.

tossups.p: The enzyme nitrogenase, which contains a cluster of iron and molybdenum atoms, turns nitrogen from the air into this compound. Bacteria living in the root nodules of legumes like peas and beans carry out that process, called nitrogen fixation.
tossups.r: Factories make this same compound using the Haber process. For 10 points, name this pungent gas.

tossups.p: In 1932, Hans Krebs and Kurt Henseleit discovered the cycle the liver uses to turn this toxic waste product into urea, the first metabolic cycle ever found. Many fish simply release this compound from their gills straight into the water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pungent compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, found in some household cleaners.

tossups.p: Water, methane, and this compound make up the hot, slushy “ices” deep inside Uranus and Neptune. The bright white zones in Jupiter’s upper atmosphere are clouds of ice made of this compound, which also forms clouds on Saturn.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound with a sharp smell, made from nitrogen and hydrogen in the Haber process.

tossups.p: Sodium metal dissolves in the liquid form of this compound to make a deep blue solution full of loose electrons. Arthur Birch used lithium or sodium in that liquid to reduce benzene rings, in a reaction named for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound, which boils at about −33 °C and is used to make fertilizer.

tossups.p: Alfred Werner founded coordination chemistry by studying cobalt chlorides bonded to different numbers of molecules of this compound. Adding this compound to a pale blue solution of copper ions produces a deep blue complex.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weak base that gains a proton to form the ammonium ion.

tossups.p: Tollens’ reagent, which coats a test tube with a silver mirror when it meets an aldehyde, is made by dissolving silver oxide in a solution of this compound. Organic compounds called amines can be thought of as this molecule with one or more of its hydrogen atoms replaced by carbon groups.
tossups.r: This compound is made on a huge scale by the Haber process. For 10 points, name this pungent gas.

tossups.p: This compound’s name traces back to the Egyptian god Amun, through the Latin name of a salt linked to one of his temples. Joseph Priestley collected this gas in the 1770s, calling it “alkaline air.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas whose molecules have one nitrogen atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms.

tossups.p: Carl von Linde’s refrigeration machines of the 1870s used this compound as their coolant, and it still chills many large industrial freezers. This compound boils at about −33 °C, unusually high for such a small molecule, because its molecules form hydrogen bonds.
tossups.r: This compound is made from nitrogen and hydrogen in the Haber process. For 10 points, name this pungent gas.

tossups.p: VSEPR theory predicts that this molecule is trigonal pyramidal, with bond angles of about 107 degrees, because a lone pair on its central atom pushes its three bonds closer together. That lone pair lets this molecule act as a Lewis base.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound of nitrogen and hydrogen, made in the Haber process.

tossups.p: Mixing this compound with chlorine bleach produces toxic gases called chloramines, so the two cleaners should never be combined. Smelling salts release this sharp-smelling gas to rouse people who have fainted.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pungent gas made by the Haber process, which turns into the ammonium ion when it gains a proton.

clues.t: A compound of one nitrogen atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms
Made from nitrogen and hydrogen gas in the Haber process, also called the Haber–Bosch process
Most of it becomes fertilizer, which helps grow food for billions of people
A colorless gas with a sharp, pungent smell, used in some household glass cleaners
A weak base that gains a proton (H⁺) to become the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺
Trigonal pyramidal shape with one lone pair and bond angles of about 107°
Its lone pair makes it a Lewis base that can bond to metal ions
Boils at about −33 °C, high for its size, because its molecules form hydrogen bonds
Meets HCl gas in a tube to make a white ring of a chloride salt closer to the HCl end, showing Graham’s law
Dissolves in water so readily that it powers the “fountain” experiment, which turns pink with phenolphthalein
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules make it using the enzyme nitrogenase
The liver turns this toxic waste into urea (the urea cycle of Krebs and Henseleit); many fish release it through their gills
Its ice forms the bright white cloud zones of Jupiter, and clouds on Saturn
Fritz Haber won the 1918 Nobel Prize for making it from its elements; Carl Bosch shared the 1931 prize for high-pressure methods
Factories make it with an iron-based catalyst at high pressure and temperature
Charles Townes built the first maser using it; its molecules flip inside out about 24 billion times a second
The Ostwald process burns it over a platinum catalyst to start making nitric acid
The Solvay process uses and recycles it to make sodium carbonate (soda ash)
Sodium dissolves in its liquid form to give a deep blue solution of loose electrons
The Birch reduction uses lithium or sodium dissolved in its liquid to reduce benzene rings
Alfred Werner founded coordination chemistry with its cobalt complexes; with copper(II) ions it makes a deep blue complex
Tollens’ reagent, the silver mirror test for aldehydes, is silver oxide dissolved in its solution
Amines are versions of it with one or more hydrogen atoms swapped for carbon groups
Its name traces back to the Egyptian god Amun, through the Latin name of a salt linked to his temple
Joseph Priestley collected the gas in the 1770s and called it “alkaline air”
Carl von Linde’s 1870s refrigerators used it as a coolant; it still chills large industrial freezers
Mixed with bleach, it makes toxic chloramines; smelling salts release it to rouse people who faint

trap.title: Not ammonium!
trap.body: Ammonium, NH₄⁺, is the ion this compound becomes after it grabs a proton, and it shows up in salts like ammonium chloride and ammonium nitrate. The two names differ by just a few letters, but a tossup asking for this gas will not accept the ion. Nitrogen is the other trap, since many clues are about nitrogen fixation and fertilizer.
trap.fix: Listen for “gas,” “molecule,” “Haber process,” “trigonal pyramidal,” or “lone pair”: that is this compound. “Ion,” “salt,” or a positive charge means ammonium. If the question asks for an element, nitrogen is the answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ammonia (accept NH3; do not accept “ammonium”)

topics.name: Carbon dioxide
topics.kicker: One carbon, two oxygens · The gas we exhale and plants take in
topics.briefing: Carbon dioxide is the gas you breathe out with every breath, and the gas plants soak up to build sugar during photosynthesis. Freeze it and you get dry ice, which skips the liquid stage and turns straight into gas. It also puts the fizz in soda, and because it traps heat in the atmosphere, scientists have tracked its rising level at a Hawaii observatory since 1958.
topics.answerHtml: Carbon dioxide (accept CO2; prompt on dry ice; do not accept “carbon monoxide”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Jan Baptist van Helmont [“HEL-mont”] called this substance “gas sylvestre,” or “wild gas,” after noticing that it came off burning charcoal and fermenting grape juice. Joseph Black later called it “fixed air” after showing that it is released when limestone is heated.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas that plants absorb during photosynthesis and animals breathe out.

tossups.p: In 1767, Joseph Priestley invented soda water by hanging a bowl of water above a fermenting vat at a brewery in Leeds, England, where this gas collected. Soft drinks fizz when opened because this gas, dissolved under pressure, comes back out of solution.
tossups.r: Plants take in this gas during photosynthesis. For 10 points, name this gas, whose solid form is called dry ice.

tossups.p: Charles David Keeling began measuring this gas at Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii in 1958, producing a sawtooth-shaped graph that rises every year. The graph’s yearly zigzag comes from plants in the Northern Hemisphere taking in this gas each spring and summer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this greenhouse gas that humans exhale and plants use in photosynthesis.

tossups.p: In 1986, a huge cloud of this gas burst out of Lake Nyos in Cameroon and flowed downhill, killing more than 1,700 people, because this gas is heavier than air. Scientists later installed pipes to pull this gas out of the lake’s deep water and prevent another disaster.
tossups.r: This gas turns limewater milky. For 10 points, name this gas, which plants take in during photosynthesis.

tossups.p: This substance’s triple point lies at about 5.1 atmospheres, so at normal air pressure it cannot exist as a liquid. Instead, its solid form sublimes directly into a gas at about −78 °C.
tossups.r: That solid is called dry ice. For 10 points, name this compound of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.

tossups.p: Companies remove caffeine from coffee beans using this compound in a supercritical state, above its critical temperature of about 31 °C. Fire extinguishers filled with this gas smother flames by pushing away the oxygen around them.
tossups.r: Plants take in this gas, and people exhale it. For 10 points, name this greenhouse gas.

tossups.p: The enzyme carbonic anhydrase, one of the fastest enzymes known, combines this gas with water in red blood cells to form bicarbonate. Most of this gas travels through the blood as bicarbonate ions until the lungs release it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas, which people breathe out and plants take in.

tossups.p: The Bohr effect describes how higher levels of this gas in the blood make hemoglobin release oxygen more easily. The level of this gas in the blood, more than the level of oxygen, is what mainly controls how fast you breathe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this waste gas that you exhale, made during cellular respiration.

tossups.p: Stalactites grow in caves when dripping water releases this dissolved gas, causing calcium carbonate to come out of solution. Bubbling this gas through limewater, a solution of calcium hydroxide, turns it milky.
tossups.r: Mixing baking soda and vinegar makes bubbles of this gas. For 10 points, name this gas whose solid form is dry ice.

tossups.p: This gas makes up about 96 percent of Venus’s thick atmosphere, causing a runaway greenhouse effect that makes Venus the hottest planet. On Mars, this gas freezes onto the polar caps each winter.
tossups.r: On Earth, plants use this gas in photosynthesis. For 10 points, name this greenhouse gas that people exhale.

tossups.p: Kumar Patel invented a powerful infrared laser in 1964 that uses this gas, and such lasers are used to cut metal and wood in factories. This linear molecule is nonpolar even though both of its bonds are polar, because the two bonds’ pulls cancel out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas made of one carbon and two oxygen atoms.

tossups.p: The enzyme RuBisCO [“roo-BISS-koh”], which may be the most abundant protein on Earth, grabs this gas at the start of the Calvin cycle. Cactuses and other CAM plants take in this gas only at night to save water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas that plants use, along with water, to make sugar during photosynthesis.

tossups.p: When this gas dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, lowering the ocean’s pH and making it harder for corals and shellfish to build their skeletons and shells. Yeast also releases this gas, which makes bread dough rise.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas, the main greenhouse gas released by burning fossil fuels.

tossups.p: In 1856, Eunice Foote showed that a glass cylinder filled with this gas grew hotter in sunlight than one filled with ordinary air. Forty years later, Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling this gas in the atmosphere would warm Earth by several degrees.
tossups.r: Plants absorb this greenhouse gas. For 10 points, name this gas, whose solid form is called dry ice.

tossups.p: After an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13 in 1970, the astronauts used tape, plastic bags, and cardboard to make square filters fit a round opening. Those filters used lithium hydroxide to soak up this gas from the cabin air.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas that people breathe out and plants take in.

Joseph Priestley invented soda water in 1767 using it from a brewery in Leeds, England

trap.title: Not carbon monoxide!
trap.body: Carbon monoxide, CO, has just one oxygen atom, and it is a poisonous gas made when fuel burns without enough oxygen. Its name differs from this compound’s by only a few letters, so a rushed buzz can lose the tossup. Dry ice is a second trap: it is this compound’s solid form, so saying “dry ice” may only earn a prompt.
trap.fix: Count the oxygens in the clues: photosynthesis, exhaling, soda fizz, limewater, and the greenhouse effect mean this compound. Carbon monoxide clues talk about car exhaust, binding tightly to hemoglobin, and home detectors that beep. If you are prompted after saying “dry ice,” give the compound’s name.
trap.line: Real answer line: Carbon dioxide (accept CO2; prompt on dry ice; do not accept “carbon monoxide”)

topics.name: Acids
topics.kicker: Proton donors that taste sour · Below 7 on the pH scale
topics.dates: Defined by Arrhenius (1884) and by Brønsted, Lowry, and Lewis (1923)
topics.briefing: Acids are the sour substances of chemistry: the tang in lemon juice, the bite of vinegar, and the powerful liquid in your stomach that helps digest food. Chemists define an acid as a substance that gives away hydrogen ions (protons), which is why acids have a pH below 7 and turn blue litmus paper red. Strong acids like sulfuric acid can burn skin, while weak ones like citric acid flavor sour candy.
topics.answerHtml: Acids (accept Brønsted–Lowry acids, Lewis acids, or Arrhenius acids; prompt on proton donors)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Antoine Lavoisier wrongly believed that all of these substances contain oxygen, which is why he gave oxygen a name meaning “former” of these substances. Humphry Davy later showed that hydrogen chloride dissolved in water is one of these substances, even though it contains no oxygen.
tossups.r: These substances turn blue litmus paper red. For 10 points, name these sour-tasting substances with a pH below 7.

tossups.p: Gilbert N. Lewis defined these substances as electron-pair acceptors, a definition that includes boron trifluoride even though it has no hydrogen to give away. In the same year, 1923, Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry defined these substances as proton donors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances that turn blue litmus paper red and react with bases to form salts.

tossups.p: Svante Arrhenius, who won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how dissolved substances break apart into ions, defined these substances as compounds that release hydrogen ions in water. Those hydrogen ions join water molecules to form hydronium ions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances with a pH below 7, found in vinegar and lemon juice.

tossups.p: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation relates a solution’s pH to the pKa of one of these substances and the ratio of its conjugate base to the original compound. A smaller pKa, or a larger dissociation constant Ka, means one of these substances is stronger.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these proton donors, which turn blue litmus paper red and taste sour.

tossups.p: Because of the leveling effect, the strongest of these substances all seem equally strong in water, since each one hands its proton to water completely. Chemists compare those strongest examples using the Hammett function instead of the pH scale.
tossups.r: Examples of these substances include HCl and H₂SO₄. For 10 points, name these proton donors with a pH below 7.

tossups.p: In 1940, George de Hevesy [“HEV-eh-shee”] dissolved two gold Nobel Prize medals in aqua regia to hide them from the Nazis. Aqua regia, which can dissolve gold, is made by mixing the nitric and hydrochloric types of these substances in a 1 to 3 ratio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these sour substances that donate protons and have a pH below 7.

tossups.p: In the 1600s, Robert Boyle noticed that these substances turn a blue dye called syrup of violets red, and he used that change to tell them apart from other substances. Litmus, a dye made from lichens, also turns red in these substances.
tossups.r: Phenolphthalein stays colorless in them. For 10 points, name these sour-tasting compounds with a pH below 7.

tossups.p: John Ray first collected a simple one of these substances in 1671 by distilling a large number of ants, so it is named for the Latin word for “ant.” Your muscles make another one of these substances, named for milk, during hard exercise.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these sour substances, which include the active ingredient in vinegar.

tossups.p: Parietal [“puh-RYE-uh-tul”] cells in the stomach lining pump out hydrogen ions to make a strong one of these substances, giving gastric juice a pH of about 2. Heartburn tablets made of calcium carbonate work by neutralizing these substances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these compounds that react with bases to form a salt and water.

tossups.p: Polyprotic examples of these substances can give away more than one proton: H₂SO₄ can give away two, and H₃PO₄, an ingredient in cola, can give away three. These substances react with active metals such as zinc to release hydrogen gas.
tossups.r: When these substances react with bases, they form water and a salt. For 10 points, name these proton donors.

tossups.p: Ralph Pearson’s HSAB theory sorts these substances and their partners into “hard” and “soft” types, predicting that hard ones pair best with hard partners. Metal ions such as Fe³⁺ act as these substances in the Lewis sense by accepting electron pairs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, which Brønsted and Lowry defined as proton donors.

tossups.p: Water is amphoteric, meaning it can behave either as one of these substances or as a base. A buffer, which resists changes in pH, can be made by mixing a weak one of these substances with its conjugate base.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these compounds with a pH below 7, such as the active ingredient in vinegar.

tossups.p: Søren Sørensen [“SUR-en-sen”] introduced the pH scale in 1909 at the Carlsberg Laboratory to express the concentration of the hydrogen ions that these substances release in water. In a titration, a base of known concentration is added to one of these substances until an indicator changes color.
tossups.r: These substances turn blue litmus paper red. For 10 points, name these sour compounds with pH values below 7.

tossups.p: Alchemists made “oil of vitriol” by heating green vitriol, an iron sulfate, and they used “aqua fortis,” or “strong water,” to separate silver from gold. Chemists call those two liquids the sulfuric and nitric kinds of these substances.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these compounds, which turn blue litmus red and donate protons.

tossups.p: George Olah won the 1994 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using extremely strong types of these substances, stronger than pure H₂SO₄, to study positively charged carbon ions. One of those extreme mixtures was named for the “magic” way it dissolved a Christmas candle.
tossups.r: Ordinary examples of these substances give foods like lemons a sour taste. For 10 points, name these proton donors.

trap.title: The class, not one example
trap.body: Tossups on this answer are packed with single examples: the HCl in your stomach, the H₂SO₄ in car batteries, the sour compound in vinegar. Blurting one specific name, like “hydrochloric acid,” is wrong when the question wants the whole class. Bases are the other trap, since clues about pH, litmus, titration, and neutralization fit both.
trap.fix: Listen for “these substances” or “these compounds” and answer with the class name. Proton donors, pH below 7, a sour taste, and blue litmus turning red mean this class; proton acceptors, pH above 7, a bitter, slippery feel, and red litmus turning blue mean bases.
trap.line: Real answer line: Acids (accept Brønsted–Lowry acids, Lewis acids, or Arrhenius acids; prompt on proton donors)

topics.name: Van der Waals forces
topics.kicker: Weak attractions between molecules · How geckos climb walls
topics.briefing: Van der Waals forces are the weak, short-range attractions that pull neighboring molecules toward each other, even molecules with no electric charge at all. They are named for Johannes Diderik van der Waals, a Dutch physicist who won the 1910 Nobel Prize for improving the ideal gas law to account for them. Each one is tiny, but billions of them working together let a gecko walk straight up a glass window.
topics.answerHtml: Van der Waals forces (accept van der Waals interactions; prompt on intermolecular forces, London dispersion forces, or dipole–dipole forces)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A gecko’s toes are covered with huge numbers of tiny hairs called setae [“SEE-tee”], which split into even tinier tips called spatulae that press close enough to a surface for these forces to hold the gecko up, even on glass.
tossups.r: These forces are generally weaker than hydrogen bonds. For 10 points, name these weak attractions between molecules, named for a Dutch physicist.

tossups.p: An equation of state has a constant a that corrects for these forces and a constant b that corrects for the volume of the molecules themselves. That equation, an improvement on the ideal gas law, earned the namesake of these forces the 1910 Nobel Prize in Physics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak attractions between neutral molecules, which include London dispersion forces and help geckos climb.

tossups.p: In the Lennard-Jones potential, the energy of attraction from these forces depends on the inverse sixth power of the distance between two molecules, while a much steeper inverse twelfth-power term describes how the molecules repel when pushed too close.
tossups.r: These forces hold the carbon sheets in graphite together. For 10 points, name these weak, short-range attractions between molecules, named for the Dutch physicist who improved the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: Willem Keesom [“KAY-sum”] described the part of these forces between two permanent dipoles, while Peter Debye [“deh-BYE”] described the part between a permanent dipole and an induced dipole. Fritz London explained a third part, which acts even between nonpolar atoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of weak intermolecular attractions named for a Dutch physicist.

tossups.p: In 2004, scientists peeled single sheets of graphene off graphite using ordinary sticky tape, which works because only these weak forces hold graphite’s sheets of carbon atoms together. Those sheets slide apart easily, so graphite makes a good dry lubricant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak attractions between molecules or layers, named for a Dutch scientist.

tossups.p: The boiling points of the noble gases rise from helium to xenon, because larger atoms with bigger, more easily distorted electron clouds feel stronger versions of these forces. These forces are the only attractions between helium atoms, which is why helium boils at about 4 kelvins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak intermolecular forces, which include the London dispersion forces between nonpolar molecules.

tossups.p: In non-contact mode, an atomic force microscope senses these forces between its sharp tip and a surface to map the surface’s shape. The Hamaker [“HAH-mah-ker”] constant describes how strongly these forces pull two larger objects, such as colloid particles, together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak attractions between molecules, which help geckos climb walls.

tossups.p: Half of the closest distance that two non-bonded atoms can approach each other defines a radius named for the same scientist as these forces. These forces are much weaker than covalent and ionic bonds, and also weaker than hydrogen bonds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak intermolecular attractions, named for a Dutch physicist who won the 1910 Nobel Prize.

tossups.p: Real gases stray from the ideal gas law at high pressures and low temperatures, partly because the ideal gas law ignores these attractions between molecules. These attractions are what let gases like nitrogen and argon condense into liquids when cooled enough.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak forces, named for the Dutch physicist who corrected the ideal gas law.

tossups.p: These forces between the long, nonpolar tails of phospholipids help hold cell membranes together, and they help stabilize the folded shapes of proteins. In DNA, these forces help the bases stack neatly on top of one another.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak attractions, which include London dispersion forces, named for a Dutch physicist.

tossups.p: The scientist these forces are named for wrote an 1873 doctoral thesis about the continuity of the gas and liquid states, which James Clerk Maxwell praised in the journal _Nature_. That scientist also described the law of corresponding states.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak intermolecular forces, which help geckos stick to walls.

tossups.p: Long, chain-shaped molecules such as octane feel stronger versions of these forces than tiny ones like methane, which is why octane is a liquid and methane is a gas at room temperature. Some of these forces arise from temporary, shifting dipoles in electron clouds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak attractions between molecules, which include London dispersion forces.

tossups.p: Crystals of iodine and of dry ice are held together mainly by these weak attractions, which is why both solids turn into gas so easily. These attractions grow stronger as molecules get bigger and have more electrons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these intermolecular forces, named for a Dutch physicist who won a Nobel Prize in 1910.

tossups.p: In physisorption, gas molecules cling weakly to a solid surface because of these forces, unlike chemisorption, which forms true chemical bonds. Activated charcoal in water filters and gas masks traps many molecules this way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these weak forces between molecules, named for a Dutch physicist who studied real gases.

tossups.p: Engineers have copied gecko feet to make “gecko tape” that sticks using these forces and peels off without leaving any residue, and NASA has tested gecko-inspired grippers for grabbing objects in space. These forces are generally the weakest attractions between molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these intermolecular forces that act even between nonpolar molecules, named for a Dutch physicist.

trap.title: Not hydrogen bonds
trap.body: Tossups on these forces often mention hydrogen bonds, the stronger attraction that gives water its high boiling point, to tempt early buzzers. London dispersion forces and dipole–dipole forces are special cases: each is one kind of these forces, so naming only one of them may earn a prompt. Saying just “intermolecular forces” also earns a prompt, since that phrase covers hydrogen bonds too.
trap.fix: Geckos, graphite layers, the constants a and b, and a Dutch physicist’s 1910 Nobel Prize point here. Hydrogen bonds need a hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine. If you are prompted, add the namesake’s name: “van der Waals.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Van der Waals forces (accept van der Waals interactions; prompt on intermolecular forces, London dispersion forces, or dipole–dipole forces)

topics.name: Lanthanides
topics.kicker: Elements 57 to 71 · The “rare earth” metals inside magnets and screens
topics.briefing: The lanthanides are the 15 metals from lanthanum to lutetium, usually shown in their own row below the main periodic table. Along with scandium and yttrium they are called the “rare earth” elements, though most are not actually rare. They are so alike that chemists struggled for over a century to separate them, and they power super-strong neodymium magnets, the colors in screens, and the motors of electric cars.
topics.answerHtml: Lanthanides (accept lanthanoids; prompt on rare earth elements, f-block elements, or inner transition metals; do not accept “actinides”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Four elements are named after the Swedish village of Ytterby, whose quarry supplied the minerals in which they were found. Three of those four, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium, belong to this series, while the fourth, yttrium, does not.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of 15 metals, from element 57 to element 71, found in the f-block.

tossups.p: A steady shrinking of atomic size across this series, caused by poor shielding from 4f electrons, makes zirconium and hafnium almost exactly the same size. That “contraction” named for this series makes those two elements very hard to separate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 15 elements that, along with scandium and yttrium, make up the rare earth elements.

tossups.p: In the early 1980s, General Motors and Sumitomo separately developed super-strong permanent magnets made of iron, boron, and neodymium, a member of this series. Magnets made with samarium, another member of this series, mixed with cobalt, keep working at even higher temperatures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of 15 elements, running from atomic number 57 to 71.

tossups.p: The only member of this series with no stable isotopes was first identified in 1945 in uranium fission products at Oak Ridge, and it was named for the Titan who stole fire from the gods.
tossups.r: Neodymium, another member, makes the strongest permanent magnets. For 10 points, name this series of rare earth elements that sits in its own row below the main periodic table, above the actinides.

tossups.p: In 1794, the Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin found a new “earth,” or oxide, containing the element yttrium, and a member of this series is named for him. That member, gadolinium, whose ion has seven unpaired electrons, is injected into patients as a contrast agent to make MRI images clearer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of 15 metals, from element 57 to element 71, often called rare earths.

tossups.p: Old color TV screens used europium, a member of this series, in their red phosphors, and euro banknotes reportedly use it in their glowing anti-counterfeiting marks. Erbium, another member, boosts the light signals that carry internet data through fiber-optic cables.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of f-block metals named for its first member, element 57.

tossups.p: Carl Auer von Welsbach [“OW-er fon VELS-bahk”] showed in 1885 that a supposed element called didymium, meaning “twin,” was really a mixture of two members of this series, praseodymium and neodymium. Glassblowers wear goggles made with didymium glass to block the yellow glare of hot sodium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of rare earth metals from element 57 to element 71.

tossups.p: Carl Gustaf Mosander named the first member of this series from a Greek word meaning “to lie hidden,” because it had been hiding in a cerium compound. Dysprosium, another member, gets its name from a Greek word meaning “hard to get.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this row of 15 elements that, along with the actinides, forms the f-block.

tossups.p: Cerium, the most abundant member of this series, is about as common in Earth’s crust as copper. Almost every member of this series forms a stable +3 ion, though cerium can also reach +4 and europium can drop to +2.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of elements numbered 57 through 71, often called rare earth metals.

tossups.p: Monazite [“MON-uh-zite”] and bastnäsite [“BAST-nuh-site”] are the main ores of these metals, and the Bayan Obo mine in Inner Mongolia holds the largest known deposit of them. By the 2000s, China was mining most of the world’s supply of these elements.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these elements, numbers 57 through 71, which include the neodymium used in magnets for electric car motors.

tossups.p: Because members of this series behave so alike chemically, chemists once needed thousands of slow crystallization steps to separate them, until Frank Spedding’s team at Iowa State developed ion-exchange methods in the 1940s.
tossups.r: Cerium is the most abundant member of this series. For 10 points, name this series of rare earth elements that sits below the main periodic table, just above the actinides.

tossups.p: One member of this series was named in 1803 for Ceres, which had been discovered two years earlier and is classified as a dwarf planet. An alloy rich in that member, mixed with iron, makes the flints that throw sparks in lighters and camping fire starters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of metals from element 57 to element 71, also called rare earth elements.

tossups.p: Chemists have debated whether this series’s last member, lutetium, or its first member belongs in group 3 of the periodic table. Lutetium was named by Georges Urbain [“oor-BAN”] for Lutetia, the ancient Roman name for Paris.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of 15 elements in the f-block, often called rare earths.

tossups.p: Holmium is named for Stockholm, and thulium is named for Thule, an old name for the far north; both belong to this series. Ytterbium, another member, is used in some of the world’s most precise atomic clocks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series that runs from atomic number 57 to atomic number 71.

tossups.p: Across this series, electrons fill the 4f subshell, which can hold up to 14 electrons. Members of this series are often placed in a separate row at the bottom of the periodic table to keep the table from getting too wide.
tossups.r: Along with the actinides, they are called inner transition metals. For 10 points, name this series of elements numbered 57 to 71.

trap.title: Not the actinides
trap.body: The actinides sit in the row just below this series, and the two rows are twins on the periodic table: both are f-block “inner transition metals” pulled out into their own rows. The actinides (elements 89 to 103) include uranium and plutonium, and all of them are radioactive. “Rare earth elements” is a near miss too, because that group also includes scandium and yttrium, so it may earn only a prompt.
trap.fix: Neodymium magnets, the Ytterby elements, the contraction that shrinks atoms, 4f orbitals, and element numbers 57 to 71 point here. Radioactivity, uranium, thorium, plutonium, 5f orbitals, and element numbers 89 to 103 point to the actinides.
trap.line: Real answer line: Lanthanides (accept lanthanoids; prompt on rare earth elements, f-block elements, or inner transition metals; do not accept “actinides”)

topics.name: Henry’s law
topics.kicker: More pressure, more dissolved gas · Why soda fizzes and divers get the bends
topics.briefing: Henry’s law, described by English chemist William Henry in 1803, says that the harder a gas presses on a liquid, the more of that gas dissolves into it. Soda makers force carbon dioxide into drinks under high pressure, so when you twist off the cap, the pressure drops and the gas fizzes back out. The same law explains the bends, a painful condition caused by nitrogen bubbles in a diver’s blood after rising to the surface too fast.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In an 1803 paper, a chemist from Manchester, England, described experiments measuring how much of several gases water would absorb at different temperatures and pressures. The rule he found works best for dilute solutions of gases that do not react with the liquid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas law stating that the amount of a gas that dissolves in a liquid is proportional to that gas’s partial pressure.

tossups.p: Washington Roebling, the chief engineer of the Brooklyn Bridge, fell seriously ill with “caisson disease” after working in pressurized chambers deep under the East River. This law explains that illness: under high pressure, extra nitrogen dissolved in the workers’ blood, then formed bubbles when they returned to normal pressure too quickly.
tossups.r: This law also explains why soda fizzes when it is opened. For 10 points, name this law about how gases dissolve in liquids.

tossups.p: In 1986, a deadly cloud of carbon dioxide burst out of Lake Nyos in Cameroon, whose deep water had held huge amounts of the dissolved gas under high pressure. This law’s constant depends on temperature, and warm liquids hold less dissolved gas than cold ones.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law which says that a gas’s solubility in a liquid is proportional to its partial pressure.

tossups.p: In a very dilute solution, the solvent follows Raoult’s [“rah-OOLZ”] law, but a dissolved gas follows this other law, which has its own proportionality constant. This law works poorly for gases such as ammonia and hydrogen chloride, which react with water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that explains why a bottle of soda fizzes when it is opened.

tossups.p: This law is exact only for very dilute solutions, so it is called a “limiting law.” When it is written C equals k P, its constant has units such as moles per liter per atmosphere.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas law, which explains why scuba divers who rise too quickly can get the bends.

tossups.p: Hyperbaric oxygen chambers rely on this law: raising the pressure around a patient who is breathing pure oxygen makes more oxygen dissolve in the patient’s blood. This law’s constant, written k-sub-H, is different for each pairing of a gas and a liquid.
tossups.r: Those chambers also treat divers who have the bends. For 10 points, name this law relating gas solubility to partial pressure.

tossups.p: As carbon dioxide builds up in the atmosphere, this law predicts that more of it will dissolve into seawater, making the oceans more acidic. This law’s constant also depends on temperature, which is why warm water holds less dissolved oxygen for fish.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that explains why soda fizzes when you twist off the cap and release the pressure.

tossups.p: On a high mountain, the partial pressure of oxygen is low, so less oxygen dissolves in a climber’s blood plasma, as this law predicts. In a dilute solution, a dissolved gas follows this law, while the solvent follows Raoult’s [“rah-OOLZ”] law instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law that explains the bends, which can strike divers who rise to the surface too quickly.

tossups.p: Environmental chemists use this law’s constant to predict how a pollutant will divide itself between a lake’s water and the air above it. That constant has a different value for every pairing of a gas and a liquid, and it changes with temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas solubility law, which explains why an open bottle of soda slowly goes flat.

tossups.p: This law’s constant, written k-sub-H, changes with temperature: warm water holds less dissolved gas than cold water. That is why tiny bubbles of air appear on the sides of a pot of water long before it boils.
tossups.r: This law is often written C equals k P. For 10 points, name this law relating how much gas dissolves in a liquid to that gas’s partial pressure.

tossups.p: Divers who breathe “nitrox,” an air mixture with extra oxygen and less nitrogen, absorb less nitrogen at depth, as this law predicts. Because each gas in air dissolves according to its own partial pressure, this law is often used together with Dalton’s law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law which explains why scuba divers who surface too quickly can get the bends.

tossups.p: Gas molecules constantly enter and leave the surface of a liquid, and once they do so at equal rates, this law gives the amount of gas that is dissolved. Soft drinks are bottled under high carbon dioxide pressure so that extra gas dissolves in them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law which says that the solubility of a gas is directly proportional to its partial pressure.

tossups.p: Every 10 meters of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure, so a diver breathing compressed air deep underwater absorbs extra nitrogen into the blood. To let that gas escape gradually, divers rise slowly and pause at decompression stops.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law which explains both the bends and the fizz that escapes when a soda bottle is opened.

tossups.p: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride do not follow this law well, because those gases react with the water they dissolve in. A chemist from Manchester, the English city where John Dalton worked, first stated this law in 1803.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law which explains why carbon dioxide bubbles out of a soda when the bottle is opened.

tossups.p: Power plants that release warm water into rivers can harm fish, since warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, an effect built into the temperature dependence of this law’s constant. That constant is different for every gas, so oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in very different amounts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law stating that the amount of a gas that dissolves in a liquid is proportional to the gas’s partial pressure.

As carbon dioxide builds up in the air, more of it dissolves into seawater, making the oceans more acidic
On a high mountain, the low partial pressure of oxygen means less oxygen dissolves in blood plasma
Hyperbaric chambers raise the pressure so more oxygen dissolves in a patient’s blood; they also treat the bends
Every 10 meters of seawater adds about one atmosphere of pressure, so deep divers absorb extra nitrogen

trap.title: Which gas law?
trap.body: Chemistry has a crowd of laws named for people, and several of them involve pressure. Boyle’s law links a gas’s pressure and volume, Dalton’s law says partial pressures add up to the total pressure, and Raoult’s law is about the vapor pressure of the solvent in a solution. Players who hear “partial pressure” and buzz with Dalton’s law lose the tossup.
trap.fix: This law is the one about how much gas dissolves in a liquid. Soda fizz, divers and the bends, dissolved oxygen in warm water, and “solubility is proportional to partial pressure” all mean this law. Say the full name, with “law” at the end.

topics.name: Ions
topics.kicker: Atoms and molecules with an electric charge · The particles in salt and nerves
topics.briefing: Michael Faraday named ions in 1834, from the Greek word for “going”: they are atoms or molecules that have gained or lost electrons, which gives them an electric charge. Atoms that lose electrons become positive cations, like the sodium in table salt, and atoms that gain electrons become negative anions, like chloride. Opposite charges attract, so ions lock together into crystals, carry electric current through salty water, and send signals along your nerves.
topics.answerHtml: Ions (accept ion; prompt on charged particles; do not accept “cations” or “anions” alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Svante Arrhenius won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for proposing that salts break apart into these particles when they dissolve, even with no electric current flowing. Peter Debye [“duh-BYE”] and Erich Hückel later described how each of these particles in a solution is surrounded by an “atmosphere” of oppositely charged ones.
tossups.r: During electrolysis, the positive ones travel to the cathode. For 10 points, name these charged atoms or molecules.

tossups.p: In 1834, William Whewell [“HYOO-el”] helped a scientist choose the name for these particles, along with the words “anode” and “cathode.” That scientist, Michael Faraday, took their name from the Greek word for “going,” because they travel toward the electrodes during electrolysis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles, which are called cations if positive and anions if negative.

tossups.p: Sodium’s plus-one version of these particles, fluoride, and a neon atom are isoelectronic, since each has 10 electrons. The positive kind of these particles is smaller than the atom it came from, while the negative kind is larger.
tossups.r: Table salt is a crystal of sodium and chloride ones. For 10 points, name these atoms that carry a charge after gaining or losing electrons.

tossups.p: In water, each of these particles is wrapped in a hydration shell: water molecules point their oxygen ends toward the positive ones and their hydrogen ends toward the negative ones. Simple negative ones get names ending in “-ide,” such as oxide and sulfide.
tossups.r: Salts conduct electricity when dissolved because these particles are free to move. For 10 points, name these charged particles, which include sodium and chloride.

tossups.p: A mass spectrometer turns molecules into these particles and then sorts them by their mass-to-charge ratio. Examples of these particles made of several atoms bonded together, such as sulfate, nitrate, and ammonium, are called polyatomic.
tossups.r: Atoms become these particles by gaining or losing electrons. For 10 points, name these charged particles, called cations when positive.

tossups.p: NASA’s Dawn spacecraft reached the asteroid Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres using engines that shoot out a beam of these particles made from xenon. During electrolysis, the positive ones move toward the cathode and the negative ones move toward the anode.
tossups.r: Michael Faraday named these particles in 1834. For 10 points, name these atoms or molecules that have an electric charge.

tossups.p: A salt bridge lets these particles flow between the two halves of a galvanic cell, keeping the charges balanced as the cell makes electricity. Salts conduct electricity when melted or dissolved, but not as solids, because these particles must be free to move.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles, which form when atoms gain or lose electrons.

tossups.p: Particles of this kind that appear unchanged on both sides of a reaction are called “spectators” and are left out of the net equation. Roman numerals show the charge of these particles in compound names such as iron(III) chloride.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these charged particles, which are called anions when they are negative.

tossups.p: Water softeners use resin beads to swap the calcium and magnesium versions of these particles for sodium ones. Examples of these particles made of several atoms, such as sulfate and nitrate, are called polyatomic.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these charged atoms or molecules, such as the sodium and chloride in seawater.

tossups.p: In a sodium chloride crystal, each of these particles is surrounded by six of the opposite charge, and lattice energy measures how tightly they hold together. Group 2 metals like magnesium form these particles with a charge of plus two.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these charged particles, which are called cations if positive and anions if negative.

tossups.p: The Debye–Hückel theory describes how each of these particles in a solution is surrounded by a cloud of oppositely charged ones. Pure water conducts electricity poorly, but dissolving a salt in it releases these particles and lets a current flow.
tossups.r: Electrolytes, like the ones in sports drinks, release these particles in water. For 10 points, name these charged particles.

tossups.p: For every two potassium particles of this kind that the sodium-potassium pump brings into a cell, it pushes three sodium ones out, which helps nerve cells send signals. Protein channels in cell membranes let these particles flow in and out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these charged atoms, which come in positive and negative varieties.

tossups.p: An atom grows larger when it becomes the negative kind of these particles and shrinks when it becomes the positive kind. Group 1 metals form these particles with a charge of plus one, while halogens form ones with a charge of minus one.
tossups.r: Metals form the positive kind by losing electrons. For 10 points, name these charged particles.

tossups.p: Acids release positive hydrogen particles of this kind, which join water molecules to form hydronium, while bases release negative hydroxide ones. The pH scale measures the concentration of the hydrogen ones in a solution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these atoms or groups of atoms that carry an electric charge after gaining or losing electrons.

tossups.p: The attraction between two of these particles follows Coulomb’s law, growing stronger as their charges increase and weaker as they move apart. Ammonium, which contains one nitrogen atom and four hydrogen atoms, is a positive polyatomic one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these charged particles, which form when atoms gain or lose electrons.

trap.title: Both kinds, not one
trap.body: These particles come in two kinds, and clues often name only one: positive cations like sodium, or negative anions like chloride. A player who hears “positive” and blurts “cations” loses the tossup when the question wants the whole family. Electrons are the other trap: atoms gain or lose them to become these particles, but electrons are not the answer.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “these particles” and mentions both charges, give the general name. Say “cations” or “anions” only when the question asks for one kind, and answer “electrons” only for “these negative subatomic particles.”

topics.name: Copper
topics.kicker: Element 29 · The reddish metal in wires, pennies, and the Statue of Liberty
topics.briefing: Copper is the reddish-orange metal in electrical wires, water pipes, and the coating on pennies, and it carries electricity better than any metal except silver. Mixing it with tin made bronze, the alloy that gave the Bronze Age its name, and the Statue of Liberty’s copper skin slowly turned green as it reacted with the air. Its symbol, Cu, comes from the Latin word cuprum, named for the island of Cyprus and its ancient mines.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Like chromium, this element breaks the usual filling order: its electron configuration ends in 3d10 4s1 instead of 3d9 4s2, because a completely full d subshell is extra stable. This element sits just above silver and gold in group 11.
tossups.r: Its plus-one and plus-two ions are called cuprous and cupric. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 29.

tossups.p: In Benedict’s test, sugars such as glucose turn this element’s blue plus-two ions into a brick-red oxide. The biuret test for proteins uses a blue sulfate of this element, which turns violet when proteins are present.
tossups.r: Mixed with tin, this metal makes bronze. For 10 points, name this reddish metal with atomic number 29.

tossups.p: Bordeaux [“bor-DOH”] mixture, a fungicide sprayed on grapevines since the 1880s, combines lime with this element’s sulfate. That sulfate forms bright blue crystals, which turn white when heated because they lose their water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, which is mixed with zinc to make brass and with tin to make bronze.

tossups.p: In a Daniell cell, a zinc electrode in zinc sulfate solution is connected to an electrode of this metal standing in a solution of its own sulfate. This metal and its group 11 neighbors, silver and gold, are called the coinage metals.
tossups.r: It conducts electricity better than every metal except silver. For 10 points, name this metal used in most electrical wires.

tossups.p: The first high-temperature superconductors, found in 1986, were cuprates, ceramics built around layers of this element’s oxide. This element’s compounds give a green or blue-green color in a flame test.
tossups.r: Its plus-two ions are called cupric. For 10 points, name this reddish metal with atomic number 29, used in most electrical wires.

tossups.p: Ötzi the Iceman, a 5,300-year-old mummy found in the Alps in 1991, carried an axe with a blade made of this metal. This metal’s most important ore is chalcopyrite, which also contains iron and sulfur.
tossups.r: This metal and tin make bronze, the alloy that named the Bronze Age. For 10 points, name this metal.

tossups.p: Butte [“BYOOT”], Montana, was nicknamed the “Richest Hill on Earth” for its mines of this metal. For decades, Arizona has produced more of this metal than any other U.S. state, and Chile has mined more of it than any other country.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this metal that is mixed with zinc to make brass.

tossups.p: Utah’s Bingham Canyon Mine, one of the largest open-pit mines in the world, digs out ore of this metal. Colorful ores of this metal include green malachite and blue azurite [“AZH-uh-rite”].
tossups.r: Outdoors, this metal slowly turns green, as on the Statue of Liberty. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 29.

tossups.p: Alchemists linked this metal to the planet Venus and to the goddess Aphrodite, who was closely tied to the island of Cyprus. That island, a major source of this metal in the ancient Mediterranean, gave this metal its name.
tossups.r: Its symbol comes from the Latin word cuprum. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 29.

tossups.p: Octopuses and horseshoe crabs have blue blood because their oxygen-carrying protein, hemocyanin [“hee-moh-SY-uh-nin”], uses this metal instead of iron. Adding ammonia to a solution of this metal’s plus-two ions produces a deep blue color.
tossups.r: This metal’s sulfate forms bright blue crystals. For 10 points, name this metal that is alloyed with tin to make bronze.

tossups.p: Doorknobs and hospital surfaces made of this metal and its alloys kill many of the bacteria that land on them. Some pots and pans have bottoms made of this metal because it spreads heat quickly and evenly.
tossups.r: It is also the usual metal in electrical wires. For 10 points, name this reddish-orange element with atomic number 29.

tossups.p: This element’s atomic mass, about 63.5, is a weighted average of its two stable isotopes, whose mass numbers are 63 and 65. Its plus-two ions give many of its compounds a blue or green color, like the blue crystals of its sulfate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, which coats U.S. pennies and makes up the skin of the Statue of Liberty.

tossups.p: The U.S. five-cent coin called the nickel is actually three-quarters this metal, and the rest is nickel. U.S. dimes and quarters have a core of this pure metal sandwiched between layers of its alloy with nickel.
tossups.r: Since 1982, U.S. pennies have been mostly zinc with a thin coating of this metal. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 29.

tossups.p: Impure slabs of this metal are purified by electrolysis, and the leftover “anode mud” often contains valuable silver and gold. The green coating that slowly forms on this metal outdoors, called a patina, protects the metal underneath.
tossups.r: That coating turned the Statue of Liberty green. For 10 points, name this metal with atomic number 29.

tossups.p: Ancient Egyptians ground up malachite, a green mineral containing this metal, to make eye paint. An alloy of this metal and zinc is used to make trumpets, tubas, and the other instruments of an orchestra’s brass section.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this reddish metal that conducts electricity better than any metal except silver.

topics.name: Nitrogen
topics.kicker: Element 7 · The gas that makes up about 78% of the air
topics.briefing: Nitrogen is the invisible gas that makes up about 78 percent of every breath you take, yet your body can’t use it straight from the air. Its two-atom molecules are held by a powerful triple bond, so it takes lightning, certain bacteria such as those in plant roots, or factories using the Haber process to break them apart and make plant food. Every protein and strand of DNA in your body contains nitrogen, and liquid nitrogen is cold enough to freeze a flower solid in seconds.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Scottish chemist Daniel Rutherford, an uncle of the novelist Sir Walter Scott, isolated this element in 1772 and called it “noxious air.” In liquid form, this element boils at about minus 196 degrees Celsius and is used to flash-freeze foods and lab samples.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7, the main gas in Earth’s atmosphere.

tossups.p: In 1790, Jean-Antoine Chaptal [“shap-TAHL”] named this element with words meaning “niter-former,” because it is found in the mineral niter, also called saltpeter. Its two-atom molecules are held together by a triple bond, one of the strongest bonds in chemistry.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas that makes up about 78 percent of Earth’s atmosphere.

tossups.p: The pnictogens [“NIK-tuh-jenz”], the group this element tops, take their name from a Greek word meaning “to choke,” because this element’s gas cannot be breathed in place of air. This element sits directly above phosphorus on the periodic table.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7, which is found in every amino acid and in the bases of DNA.

tossups.p: An enzyme containing iron and molybdenum [“muh-LIB-duh-num”] lets certain bacteria break apart the very stable molecules of this element. Bacteria in the root nodules of legumes such as peas, beans, and clover “fix” this element from the air so that plants can use it.
tossups.r: Fertilizers are packed with this element. For 10 points, name this gas that makes up most of Earth’s air.

tossups.p: In the Ostwald process, ammonia reacts with oxygen over a platinum catalyst, the first step in making an acid that contains this element. That ammonia comes from the Haber process, which combines hydrogen with this element taken from the air.
tossups.r: Plants need this element to grow. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7.

tossups.p: Lord Rayleigh noticed that this element taken from the air was slightly denser than this element made from chemicals, a puzzle that led to the discovery of argon. Bags of potato chips are filled with this gas to keep the chips fresh.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this colorless gas that makes up about 78 percent of Earth’s atmosphere.

tossups.p: High in the atmosphere, neutrons from cosmic rays strike atoms of this element’s most common isotope, which has a mass number of 14, and turn them into carbon-14. Lightning splits molecules of this element so that its atoms can combine with oxygen and fall to the ground in rain.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element found in every protein and in the bases of DNA.

tossups.p: Ernest Rutherford carried out the first artificial transmutation of one element into another by hitting atoms of this element with alpha particles, turning some of them into oxygen. Many car airbags inflate with this gas, which a reaction of sodium azide releases in a split second.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7, which makes up most of Earth’s air.

tossups.p: This element makes up most of the thick, hazy atmosphere of Titan, Saturn’s largest moon. Some soil bacteria return this element to the air as a gas, completing a cycle named for this element.
tossups.r: Other soil bacteria turn ammonia into nitrites and nitrates. For 10 points, name this gas that makes up about 78 percent of Earth’s atmosphere.

tossups.p: Chile fought Peru and Bolivia in the War of the Pacific from 1879 to 1884 over desert deposits of saltpeter, a compound of this element used in fertilizer and explosives. Explosives such as TNT and gunpowder get their power from compounds of this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7, the main gas in the air.

tossups.p: Deep-sea divers breathing compressed air can feel dizzy and confused from narcosis, nicknamed “rapture of the deep,” caused by the high pressure of this gas. If those divers rise too quickly, bubbles of this gas form in their blood.
tossups.r: That condition is called the bends. For 10 points, name this element, the main gas in air.

tossups.p: Ice made mostly of this element fills Sputnik Planitia, the western half of the bright heart-shaped region on Pluto, and Voyager 2 saw geysers of this element’s gas on Neptune’s moon Triton. A brown oxide of this element, released by car engines, helps form smog.
tossups.r: Plants get this element from fertilizers. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7.

tossups.p: Antoine Lavoisier [“lah-vwah-zee-AY”] named this element “azote,” from Greek words meaning “without life,” because it cannot keep an animal alive. Its two-atom molecules are held by a triple bond so strong that the gas is very unreactive.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7, which makes up about 78 percent of the air.

tossups.p: A 1998 Nobel Prize honored the discovery that a small gas molecule made of one atom of this element and one atom of oxygen signals blood vessels to relax. In liquid form, this element is cold enough to freeze a flower solid in seconds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas that makes up about 78 percent of Earth’s air.

tossups.p: Fertilizer runoff rich in this element feeds algal blooms that can leave “dead zones,” areas of lakes and coastal waters with too little oxygen for fish. Bacteria living in the root nodules of peas and beans turn this element from the air into a form plants can use.
tossups.r: Its gas makes up about 78 percent of the air. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 7.
