trap.body: Nitrogen tossups are full of its famous compounds, like ammonia from the Haber process, nitrates in fertilizer, and nitroglycerin in dynamite, and players blurt the compound instead of the element. Oxygen is the other trap: it is the second most common gas in air, about 21 percent, and it sits right next door on the periodic table.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this element” or “this gas,” name the element itself. Atomic number 7, about 78 percent of the air, a triple bond, root nodules, azote, and Daniel Rutherford all point here; oxygen is element 8, the gas we need to breathe, and the one that makes fires burn.

topics.name: Vapor pressure
topics.kicker: Push of a liquid’s own gas · When it matches the air’s, the liquid boils
topics.briefing: When you put a liquid in a closed jar, some of its molecules escape into the space above and push on the walls as a gas, and that push is the liquid’s vapor pressure. It climbs as the liquid warms, and when it matches the pressure of the air around it, the liquid boils, which is why water boils at a lower temperature on a mountaintop. Liquids with high vapor pressures, like nail polish remover, evaporate fast and fill a room with their smell.
topics.answerHtml: Vapor pressure (accept vapour pressure, equilibrium vapor pressure, or saturation vapor pressure; prompt on pressure or partial pressure; do not accept “boiling point”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Clausius–Clapeyron [“klah-pay-RAWN”] equation uses a liquid’s enthalpy of vaporization to predict how this quantity changes with temperature. Liquids with strong intermolecular forces, such as water with its hydrogen bonds, have relatively low values of this quantity.
tossups.r: A liquid boils when this quantity equals the pressure of the surrounding air. For 10 points, name this quantity, the pressure of the gas above a liquid.

tossups.p: The Antoine [“an-TWAHN”] equation, which uses three constants named A, B, and C, is a formula for how this quantity rises with temperature. For a pure liquid, this quantity depends only on the temperature, not on how much liquid is present or how big its container is.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which equals one atmosphere at a liquid’s normal boiling point.

tossups.p: A manometer attached to a sealed flask with its air pumped out can measure this quantity for a liquid placed inside. At 100 degrees Celsius, water’s value of this quantity reaches 760 millimeters of mercury, or one atmosphere, but at room temperature it is only a small fraction of that.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the pressure of the gas that escapes from a liquid in a closed container once escaping and returning molecules balance.

tossups.p: According to the Kelvin equation, this quantity is higher above a tiny, curved droplet than above a flat surface of the same liquid. Relative humidity compares the amount of water in the air to water’s value of this quantity at that temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that rises with temperature and equals the outside pressure when a liquid boils.

tossups.p: In the Bergeron process, ice crystals in a cloud grow while supercooled water droplets shrink, because ice has a lower value of this quantity than liquid water at the same temperature.
tossups.r: Mothballs and dry ice have high values of it. For 10 points, name this quantity, which is high for volatile liquids like acetone.

tossups.p: Diethyl ether, whose molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, has a far higher value of this quantity than water at room temperature. Volatile liquids, like the acetone in nail polish remover, have high values of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that equals atmospheric pressure when a liquid boils.

tossups.p: Mixtures that stray far from Raoult’s [“rah-OOLZ”] law can form azeotropes [“ay-ZEE-uh-trohps”], which boil without changing composition. Raoult’s law itself says that a solvent’s value of this quantity equals its mole fraction times the value for the pure solvent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity which rises with temperature until it equals the outside pressure and the liquid boils.

tossups.p: Fractional distillation works because the liquid with the higher value of this quantity makes up more of the gas rising from a boiling mixture. Dissolving salt or sugar in water lowers this quantity, a colligative property that also raises water’s boiling point.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity exerted by the gas above a liquid in a closed container.

tossups.p: The nearly empty space at the top of a mercury barometer actually holds a tiny amount of mercury gas, set by mercury’s very low value of this quantity. When chemists collect a gas over water, they subtract water’s value of this quantity from the total pressure.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which equals atmospheric pressure at a liquid’s boiling point.

tossups.p: Freeze-drying lowers the surrounding pressure below the value of this quantity for ice, so the frozen water in food turns straight into a gas. On a phase diagram, the curve separating liquid from gas traces this quantity and ends at the critical point.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which rises with temperature and is high for liquids that evaporate quickly.

tossups.p: When the pressure in a fast-moving liquid drops below this quantity, bubbles suddenly form and collapse, a process called cavitation that can damage ship propellers. Liquids that evaporate quickly, such as gasoline, are called volatile because this quantity is high for them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which equals the air pressure when a liquid boils.

tossups.p: Room-temperature water in a sealed jar begins to boil when a pump removes enough air that the pressure inside drops to this quantity. In the same way, water boils below 100 degrees Celsius on a high mountain, where the air presses down less.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the pressure of the gas above a liquid at equilibrium.

tossups.p: Air that cools to its dew point becomes saturated: the pressure from the water it holds has reached water’s value of this quantity at that temperature, so dew or fog begins to form. At that point the relative humidity reaches 100 percent.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that rises as a liquid warms, until the liquid boils.

tossups.p: Inside a pressure cooker, water stays liquid until this quantity climbs to about twice normal air pressure, at roughly 120 degrees Celsius, so food cooks faster. This quantity is the same for a teaspoon of water or a whole lake at the same temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, which rises with temperature and equals atmospheric pressure at a liquid’s boiling point.

tossups.p: A spray can with a liquefied propellant keeps nearly the same pressure until it is almost empty, because the liquid keeps refilling the space above it with gas at a steady value of this quantity. Adding a nonvolatile solute like sugar to water lowers this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity that equals the outside pressure when a liquid boils.

trap.title: Not the boiling point
trap.body: This quantity and the boiling point are tied together, so tossups on one are full of clues about the other. A liquid boils at the temperature where this quantity equals the outside pressure, so a clue like “reaches 760 millimeters of mercury at 100 °C” tempts players to say “boiling point.” But the boiling point is a temperature, and this answer is a pressure.
trap.fix: Check what the question asks for. “This temperature” means the boiling point. “This quantity” that rises with temperature, follows Raoult’s law, or drops when a solute dissolves means this answer. Say both words: plain “pressure” only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Vapor pressure (accept vapour pressure; prompt on pressure; do not accept “boiling point”)

topics.name: Sulfuric acid
topics.kicker: The “king of chemicals” · The most-made industrial chemical in the world
topics.briefing: Sulfuric acid is so important to industry that it is nicknamed the “king of chemicals,” and the world makes more of it than any other industrial chemical, for uses from fertilizer to car batteries. Alchemists called it “oil of vitriol.” It grabs water so fiercely that it turns sugar into a steaming black column of carbon, and mixing it with water releases so much heat that chemists always add the acid to the water, never the reverse.
topics.answerHtml: Sulfuric acid (accept sulphuric acid, H2SO4, or oil of vitriol; prompt on vitriol; do not accept “sulfurous acid”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1831, British vinegar merchant Peregrine Phillips patented a way to make this compound in which sulfur dioxide and oxygen react over a hot catalyst. Modern versions of that method, the contact process, use vanadium oxide as the catalyst to make sulfur trioxide.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong acid whose molecules contain two hydrogen atoms, one sulfur atom, and four oxygen atoms.

tossups.p: Johann Glauber [“GLOU-ber”] made hydrochloric acid by heating table salt with this acid, leaving behind sodium sulfate, later called Glauber’s salt. When this acid loses just one of its two hydrogen ions, it becomes the hydrogen sulfate ion, also called bisulfate.
tossups.r: Its salts are called sulfates. For 10 points, name this strong acid, nicknamed the “king of chemicals.”

tossups.p: Mixing this acid with hydrogen peroxide makes “piranha solution,” which chemists use to strip stubborn grime off glassware. This acid pulls water out of table sugar so strongly that the sugar swells into a steaming black column of carbon.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this acid used in car batteries, whose salts are called sulfates.

tossups.p: Mixed with nitric acid, this acid produces the nitronium ion, which chemists use to make explosives such as TNT. This acid soaks up water from the air so eagerly that chemists use it to dry gases.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong acid made by the contact process, the most-produced industrial chemical in the world.

tossups.p: Drops of this acid speed up Fischer esterification, which joins an alcohol and a carboxylic acid into a sweet-smelling ester. Reacting this acid with zinc metal releases hydrogen gas and leaves behind zinc sulfate.
tossups.r: This acid is made by the contact process. For 10 points, name this strong acid, the electrolyte in lead–acid car batteries.

tossups.p: In 1746, John Roebuck began making this acid on a large scale inside huge chambers lined with lead, a metal it barely attacks. That lead chamber process used nitrogen oxides to help turn sulfur dioxide into this acid.
tossups.r: A hydrometer measures the strength of this acid to check a car battery’s charge. For 10 points, name this strong acid.

tossups.p: Concentrated samples of this acid are colorless and oily, and about 1.8 times as dense as water. Mixing this acid with water gives off so much heat that chemists always add the acid to the water, never the other way around, to avoid dangerous splattering.
tossups.r: Venus’s clouds are made of droplets of this acid. For 10 points, name this strong acid, whose salts are called sulfates.

tossups.p: After Mount Pinatubo [“pee-nuh-TOO-boh”] erupted in 1991, droplets of this acid formed in the stratosphere and cooled Earth slightly for the next couple of years. Venus is wrapped in thick clouds made of droplets of this acid.
tossups.r: Sulfur dioxide from burning coal turns into this acid in the air, causing acid rain. For 10 points, name this strong acid, the electrolyte in car batteries.

tossups.p: This acid gives up its first hydrogen ion completely in water, but its second one comes off much less easily, so the hydrogen sulfate ion it forms is a weaker acid. More of this acid goes into making phosphate fertilizers than into any other product.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this acid made from sulfur, which is produced in greater amounts than any other industrial chemical.

tossups.p: A country’s output of this chemical was once used as a measure of its industrial strength. In the last step of making this acid, sulfur trioxide is dissolved in concentrated acid to form oleum, because adding it straight to water creates a hard-to-control mist.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong acid that makes up the electrolyte in car batteries.

tossups.p: In each molecule of this acid, a central sulfur atom sits at the middle of a tetrahedron of four oxygen atoms, two of which carry hydrogen atoms. This acid is a powerful dehydrating agent that can char wood, paper, and cloth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong acid, the most-produced industrial chemical in the world.

tossups.p: Steel can be “pickled” in this acid to strip away rust and scale before it is coated. Chemistry teachers warn students to add this acid to water, never water to the acid, because mixing them gives off so much heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong acid made by the contact process, nicknamed the “king of chemicals.”

tossups.p: Alchemists made this acid by heating green crystals of iron sulfate, a mineral then known as green vitriol. This acid turns table sugar into a tall, steaming black column of carbon by pulling the water out of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this strong acid whose molecules contain two hydrogen atoms, one sulfur atom, and four oxygen atoms.

tossups.p: Treating phosphate rock with this acid produces a fertilizer called superphosphate. In the contact process used to make this acid, sulfur dioxide reacts with oxygen over a vanadium oxide catalyst.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this acid, which forms in polluted air from sulfur dioxide and falls to the ground in acid rain.

tossups.p: One mole of this acid has a mass of about 98 grams. Its salts include Epsom salt, which is magnesium sulfate, and gypsum, which is calcium sulfate, the mineral in plaster and drywall.
tossups.r: Reacting this acid with zinc gives off bubbles of hydrogen gas. For 10 points, name this strong acid that fills car batteries.

trap.title: Sulfuric, not sulfurous
trap.body: Sulfur makes several compounds with look-alike names. Sulfurous acid has one fewer oxygen atom and forms when sulfur dioxide dissolves in water, and hydrogen sulfide is a gas that smells like rotten eggs. Mixing up the endings “-ic” and “-ous” names a different acid, so it loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Count the oxygens. Four oxygen atoms, the contact process, oleum, car batteries, and the “king of chemicals” all mean this acid; three oxygen atoms means sulfurous acid. Say the whole name, ending in “-ic acid.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Sulfuric acid (accept H2SO4 or oil of vitriol; do not accept “sulfurous acid”)
